title: A study to determine the key surgical and patient factors for early, safe discharge after total knee replacement in the NHS
summary:
Background and study aims 
As part of normal care after surgery for a total knee replacement for arthritis, it is important that pain is kept under control, patients can get up and move, and that discharge home is safe.  We know that a shorter stay in hospital after an operation is associated with a lower risk of complications.  However, recovery in hospital involves many different aspects – patients need to recover from their anaesthetic, have their pain controlled, be able to get up and walk, and have any equipment in place before discharge home.

This study is looking at getting patients home on the same day as their operation. This already happens for some operations at Newcastle, and for knee replacements in other parts of the country. We will be linking together our most up-to-date techniques for surgery, anaesthetics and rehabilitation.

Who can participate? 
Adult patients diagnosed with osteoarthritis (wear and tear) of the knee and are awaiting a knee replacement. 

What does the study involve? 
Participants will be asked to sign a consent form and to answer some questions about their knee and their general health. These questions will be asked again six weeks, six months, one year and two years after their operation to see how their recovery is progressing.

Surgery will be planned and carried out as normal. Participants will have a spinal anaesthetic (with sedation if needed), not a general anaesthetic. This is the standard anaesthetic for knee replacements at Newcastle. A spinal anaesthetic has fewer side effects for things like pain and vomiting, which can help patients moving quicker.

The surgery will be robotic-assisted – the surgeon is in full control of the robot, but it helps the cuts in the bone to be more accurate. Robotic-assisted knee replacements have been carried out at Newcastle for over five years.

After the operation, participants will be looked after by physiotherapists, occupational therapists and nurses, who will help them to get up and walk, and check they are safe and well to go home. If it is not safe for them to go home, then they will be able to stay in the hospital. Participants will not be discharged until it is safe to do so.

Same-day discharge is already safely used for a variety of operations. The criteria for someone to go home on the same day as their operation are very similar to the criteria for someone to stay in the hospital overnight.

In particular, we will make sure:
•	Pain is under control
•	Blood pressure is good, and they don’t feel dizzy or sick
•	Can stand up and walk (with appropriate walking aids)
•	Can safely get in and out of bed
•	Can safely walk up and down the stairs (if they have stairs at home)
•	Have someone to stay with them at home for at least 24 hours

Blood tests - bloods samples will be taken in a subgroup of 24 participants, taken at baseline and 2 weeks post-surgery. They will look at markers of surgical stress

Urine tests - urine samples will be taken in a different subgroup of 24 participants, taken at baseline and 2 weeks post-surgery. They will also look at markers of surgical stress

X-rays and CT scans – there will be no extra X-rays or scans as part of the study 

Activity monitoring - activity monitoring will be carried out in a subgroup of 36 patients. Activity data will be collected for 7 consecutive days using a wristwatch-style device. The data will be collected at baseline, immediately post-surgery and 8 weeks post-surgery

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
There are no specific benefits to taking part in this study, but participants will receive the most up-to-date treatment in terms of surgery, anaesthetics and rehabilitation. They will also be seen by specialist staff throughout their stay, and be followed up more closely. The information we collect will also help us to improve services for patients in the future.

There are very few risks from taking part. There are two extra blood tests, which can be uncomfortable. All x-rays and scans are part of routine care, so there is no additional radiation. 

Where is the study run from?  
The Newcastle upon Tyne Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
April 2026 to July 2028.

Who is funding the study? 
Stryker Europe.

Who is the main contact?
Prof David Deehan, david.deehan@nhs.net
conditions: To compare same-day discharge rates in a case series of patients undergoing primary total knee replacement (TKR)

interventions.name: This study builds upon current work in the field of robotic joint replacement by examining the safety, economic benefit, logistics and patient outcomes for a pilot study of 120 patients undergoing proposed day case robotic-assisted knee arthroplasty. criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
All of the following must apply:
1. Listed for elective primary TKR for end stage osteoarthritis under the care of three participating surgeons
2. Considered eligible for same-day discharge by anaesthetist
3. Male or female, aged 30–80 years at the time of listing for surgery
4. Suitable candidate for a cruciate retaining TKR (Triathlon prosthesis)
Exclusion criteria:
None of the following can apply:
1. Incompetent medial collateral ligament (MCL, grade III in laxity) observed by consultant on examination
2. Patient is unable to comply with the study protocol (incl. refusal for CT scan)
3. Female participants who is pregnant, lactating or planning pregnancy during the course of the study
4. Requires patella resurfacing
5. Inability to understand the patient information for the study, provide written informed consent or answer study questionnaires for cognitive or language reasons
